notes.meaning: David attacked and subdued the Philistines, who had troubled Israel for many generations. He captured Metheg-ammah, a phrase meaning 'the bridle of the mother city,' which refers to the Philistine capital of Gath and its surrounding towns. By taking control of this city, David took the reins of power away from the Philistines and gave Israel lasting relief from their attacks.

David defeated the Moabites and ordered the captured soldiers to lie down in a row to be measured with a cord. Two lengths of the cord were marked for death, while one full length was spared to live and work the land. The surviving Moabites became David's subjects and paid regular tribute money, fulfilling the ancient prophecy that a ruler from Israel would strike Moab.

David marched north and defeated King Hadadezer of Zobah. This Syrian king had set out to expand or recover his power toward the Euphrates River, but David stopped him. By winning this battle, David extended Israel's influence all the way to the border God had promised to Abraham.

David captured a great number of chariots, horsemen, and foot soldiers from Hadadezer. He disabled almost all the captured warhorses by cutting their leg tendons, keeping only enough horses for one hundred chariots. By doing this, David obeyed God's command that Israel's kings must not pile up horses, showing he trusted in the Lord rather than military power.

The Arameans of Damascus came to help King Hadadezer, but David fought them and killed twenty-two thousand soldiers. Damascus was a powerful Syrian city, but joining an alliance against God's people only brought about their defeat.

David placed military posts inside the territory of Damascus and made the Syrian people his servants who paid regular tribute. The key to David's success was not his own military genius, but that the Lord protected him and gave him victory wherever he marched.

David took the gold shields carried by Hadadezer's royal officers and brought them back to Jerusalem. He did not use this wealth for personal vanity, but kept it as a trophy of God's power over the nations.

David also took a large amount of bronze from Betah and Berothai, two cities that belonged to Hadadezer. This great store of metal was carefully preserved and later used by his son Solomon to build the large bronze basin and vessels for the temple.

King Toi of Hamath learned that David had crushed Hadadezer's entire army. Because Hadadezer had been Toi's bitter enemy, Toi sent his son Joram to greet David, congratulate him on his victory, and ask for peace. Joram presented rich gifts of silver, gold, and bronze to secure a friendly alliance with the new king of Israel.

David dedicated all of Toi's gifts to the Lord, along with the silver and gold taken from all the nations he had conquered. This included spoils from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Philistia, Amalek, and Zobah. Instead of enriching himself, David set this treasure apart so it could one day be used to build the house of God.

David gained great fame when his army struck down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, south of the Dead Sea. Even though his generals led the fighting on the field, David gave God the credit for their courage and triumph.

David stationed military garrisons throughout all of Edom, bringing the entire nation under his rule. This victory fulfilled God's ancient promise that the older brother Esau would serve Jacob. The passage repeats that David's unending success came because the Lord gave him victory wherever he went.

David ruled over the entire nation of Israel with fairness and righteousness for all his people. He listened to their appeals and gave honest rulings without showing favoritism to the rich or denying justice to the poor. His fair and caring leadership pointed ahead to the perfect rule of Christ.

David chose capable officials to help him run the kingdom smoothly. Joab was appointed commander-in-chief over the whole army, while Jehoshaphat served as the royal recorder. The recorder kept official state histories and reminded the king of important matters that needed his attention.

Zadok and Ahimelech carried out the sacred duties of the high priesthood, serving the Lord at the sanctuary and before the ark. Seraiah served as the royal scribe, working as a secretary of state who wrote official decrees and handled public documents.

Benaiah was placed in command of the Cherethites and Pelethites, who served as the king's personal bodyguard and trusted runners. David's sons were also given positions of honor, serving as chief rulers and close advisers beside the king.
